Title: Halogenated Trityl Cations as Easy‐to‐Access Super Electrophiles
Text:
Carbocations Hot Paper
Halogenated Trityl Cations as Easy-to-Access Super Electrophiles
Johanna Schlögl, Amelie L. Brosius, Ahmet N. Toraman, Anja Wiesner, Simon Steinhauer,
Carsten Müller, and Sebastian Riedel*
Dedicated to Hermann-Josef Frohn on the occasion of his 80th birthday.
Abstract: Herein, we present the easy-to-access syn-
thesis of the perfluorotrityl cation (15F+) with commer-
cial GaCl3 and the further functionalization of the para-
fluorine atoms of 15F+ via halodefluorination using
trimethylsilyl halides TMSX (X=Cl, Br). This gives
access to equally reactive halogenated trityl derivatives
(p-3Cl12F+ and p-3Br12F+), which can be handled at
room temperature. The impact of the para-exchange on
the electronic structure is determined by NMR and UV/
Vis
spectroscopy.
Finally,
the
new
synthons’
high
hydride ion affinities are demonstrated computationally
and experimentally by hydride abstraction from the
short-chain, linear alkanes n-pentane and n-butane.
Hydride abstraction is a versatile yet challenging tool in
synthesis due to its role in generating highly reactive species
such
as
carbocations
or
other
positively
charged
intermediates.[1] The latter are key compounds in many
organic and inorganic reactions, which are not only of
academic interest, but may also be industrially relevant.[2] A
common reaction for such a hydride abstraction is often
realized by the so-called trityl cation [C(C6H5)3]+ (in the
following abbreviated as 15H+).[3] The three phenyl groups
stabilize the positively charged central carbon atom and the
relatively bulky ligands allow for its isolation.[2c] Due to the
electron-deficient nature of the central carbon atom, the
trityl cation is an effective reagent for hydride and alkyl
abstractions and serves as a one-electron oxidant. However,
as shown previously, its hydride ion affinity (HIA) can be
further increased by fluorination of the phenyl moieties.[4]
The perfluorinated counterpart [C(C6F5)3]+ (in the following
abbreviated as 15F+) shows a considerably higher HIA
([C(C6F5)3]+ =955 kJmol� 1) than the non-fluorinated trityl
cation
([C(C6H5)3]+ =801 kJmol� 1).
Even
though
[C(C6F5)3]+ was first characterized by NMR spectroscopy in
the 1960s by Filler and Olah as an intermediate in chemical
reactions,
its
first
isolation
was
not
achieved
until
recently.[5–7] This was made possible by introducing the very
robust
and
weakly
coordinating
anion
(WCA)
[Al-
(OTeF5)4]� .[7] At the same time, a series of partially
fluorinated trityl cations had been reported by Ozerov et al.
as
carborane-stabilized
salts.[8a]
Beforehand,
a
partially
fluorinated trityl cation was already isolated by Reed et al.,
but not investigated further.[8b]
The very high electrophilicity of the perfluorinated trityl
cation was proven experimentally when it enabled the
generation of the tert-butyl cation through hydride ion
abstraction from isobutane and showed its high oxidation
potential by the synthesis of a magic blue derivative.[7] Very
recently, it was shown that fluorinated chloronium ions
could even exceed the hydride ion affinity by more than
100 kJmol–1 and can activate short-chain, linear alkanes, e.g.,
n-pentane.[9]
However, the synthetic access and application of these
fluorinated trityl cations and chloronium ions have been
limited so far by their synthetic accessibility due to the non-
commonly available WCAs. As M. Ingleson recently pointed
out, “a simpler route to access these fluorinated trityl salts
would be really useful for the community”.[10]
Hence, our group has developed an easier and more
straightforward way to prepare this compound. Herein, we
present the easy-to-access synthesis of the perfluorotrityl
cation (15F+) and the further functionalization of its para-
fluorine atoms via halodefluorination using trimethylsilyl
halides TMSX (X=Cl, Br). This enables the synthesis of
more stable yet equally reactive halogenated trityl deriva-
tives (p-3Cl12F+ and p-3Br12F+). Right before the publica-
tion of this work, an article by Ozerov et al. has been
published that reports on the stabilization of the perfluoro-
trityl cation at room temperature using halogenated carbor-
ane WCAs.[8c]
The addition of 0.5 equivalents of PhF
3CCl to a colorless
solution of GaCl3 in SO2ClF at � 80°C results in an
immediate color change to berry-red and the appearance of
three signals in the low-temperature 19F NMR spectrum at
� 108.7, � 123.7, and � 150.9 ppm (Scheme 1, Figure S1).
These signals can be assigned to the para-, ortho-, and meta-
fluorine atoms of 15F+. The UV/Vis spectrum shows an
absorption maximum at 497 nm, which fits the literature-
reported value (Figure S4).[5]

temperatures lead to the appearance of new signals in the
19F NMR spectrum at � 126.0 and � 131.5 ppm (Figure S3).
They belong to a side product formed via the reaction of
15F+ with an unidentified gallium-chloro species, leading to
a step-wise chlorodefluorination at the para-position of the
three phenyl moieties. Intrigued by this observation, we
turned our attention towards the controlled halodefluorina-
tion of 15F+. For this purpose, a halide transfer reagent with
a covalently bound nucleophile was required, as ionic
sources were found to recover the corresponding trityl
halide. We opted for trimethylsilyl halides TMSX (X=Cl,
Br), which offer the additional advantage of producing
gaseous trimethylsilyl fluoride during the reaction. Chlor-
odefluorination reactions using trialkylsilyl chlorides have
been recently reported for other systems.[11]

3.5
equivalents of trimethylsilyl chloride were added and the
reaction mixture was brought to � 25°C and stirred for 30
minutes, which led to a color change from berry-red to violet
(Scheme 1, Figure 1). Analysis of the solution by low-
temperature NMR spectroscopy confirmed the full con-
sumption of 15F+. It revealed two new signals at � 126.0 and
� 131.5 ppm, corresponding to the ortho- and meta- fluorine
atoms of the para-chlorinated derivative p-3Cl12F+ (Fig-
ure S5). The
13C{19F} NMR spectrum shows the expected
shift of 172.2 ppm for the central carbon atom of the cationic
species (Figure S6). The UV/Vis spectrum displays an
absorption maximum at 543 nm (Figure S7). Warming the
solution to room temperature does not lead to any further
color change or shift in the UV/Vis spectrum. However, no
signals corresponding to p-3Cl12F+ or any kind of decom-
position product were detected in the 19F NMR spectrum.
This observation may be attributed to the formation of small
amounts of radical species, not detectable by NMR due to
their paramagnetic nature, that engage in dynamic single
electron transfer (SET) processes with p-3Cl12F+, rendering
the latter NMR silent. Similar observations have been
described
in
the
literature.[12]
Re-cooling
the
reaction
mixture leads to the reappearance of the signals correspond-
ing to p-3Cl12F+. Interestingly, over the course of a few
weeks single crystals suitable for single crystal X-ray analysis
grew from a concentrated solution of p-3Cl12F+ in SO2ClF
at room temperature. The obtained structure revealed a
further halodefluorination in the ortho-positions of the
phenyl moieties resulting in 9Cl6F+ (Figure 2). It seems that
one equivalent of GaCl3 has reacted with p-3Cl12F+,
presumably following an analogous mechanism as the one
previously described leading to a stepwise chlorodefluorina-
tion in solutions of 15F+ (Figure S3). 9Cl6F+ reveals a
planar environment for the central carbon atom with the
aryl rings arranged in a propeller-like fashion. The sum of
the angles around the central carbon atom is 360.1(4)°. This
is
in
line
with
the
reported
molecular
structure
for

For the bromodefluorination of 15F+ the same proce-
dure was applied, this time using trimethylsilyl bromide
(Scheme 1). During the reaction the color changes from
berry-red to blue-violet (Figure 1). The corresponding low-
temperature
19F NMR spectrum shows only one signal at
� 133.3 ppm, due to the isochronous nature of the ortho- and
meta- fluorine atoms of the generated para-brominated
derivative p-3Br12F+ (Figure S8). This behavior might occur
due to the presence of traces of the corresponding radical
species.
However, the
13C{19F} NMR spectrum shows the ex-
pected five signals and the low field shifted signal for the
central carbon atom of the cationic species at 175.4 ppm
(Figure S9). The UV/Vis spectrum displays an absorption
maximum at 566 nm (Figure S10). As for its chlorinated
derivative, room temperature solutions of p-3Br12F+ are
NMR silent, though their color and UV/Vis absorption
spectrum remain unchanged. Re-cooling a solution of
p-3Br12F+ leads to the reappearance of the respective
signals.
In summary, this indicates that both p-3Cl12F+ and
p-3Br12F+ can be handled at room-temperature in SO2ClF
for at least one or two days as opposed to their perfluori-
nated analogs.
The impact of the halodefluorination in the para-
position of the phenyl moieties can be observed with NMR
spectroscopy and UV/Vis absorption spectroscopy (Table 1).
In case of the latter, the absorption maximum is red-shifted,
going from 15F+ over p-3Cl12F+ to p-3Br12F+ (Figure 1).
This red shift is further supported by DFT calculations at
the B3LYP� D3(BJ)/def2-TZVPP level, which show a de-
crease in the HOMO–LUMO energy gap upon the exchange
of
the
para-fluorine
ligand
for
the
heavier
halogens
(Table 1). Regarding the 13C chemical shifts, the strongest
impact of the substitution is found for the para-carbon
atoms directly bound to the different halogens, whose
signals are strongly high-field shifted going from � F to � Cl
to � Br (Table 1, Figure S11). This trend is known as Normal
Halogen Dependence (NHD) and can be explained by an
increased shielding of the carbon center with increasing
nuclear charge, mainly due to spin-orbit coupling.[13–15] The
effect is more pronounced for bromine than for chlorine.
Moreover, the δ(13C) signals of the ortho- and meta-carbon
atoms move closer together as the fluorine ligand gets
exchanged for chlorine or bromine. A similar trend can be
observed in the 19F NMR spectra, where the signals of the
ortho- and meta-fluorine atoms even become isochronous
for p-3Br12F+ (Figure S5, S8).
As theoretically predicted by Couchman et al. and
experimentally verified by our group, the perfluorinated
trityl cation possesses an enormous hydride ion affinity,
surpassing that of 15H+.[4,7] To assess the HIA of the
halogenated trityl derivatives p-3Cl12F+ and p-3Br12F+,
DFT calculations were performed at the B3LYP� D3(BJ)/
def2-TZVPP level using trimethyl silane as the anchor
system (Table 2).[16–19] The obtained values are comparable
to the perfluorinated analog‘s, suggesting similar reactivities
for p-3Cl12F+, p-3Br12F+, and 15F+. A similar outcome is
observed for the fluoride (FIA) and chloride ion affinity
(CIA) (Table 2). The small impact of the para-substitution
on the electrophilicity of the overall molecule was already
described by Couchman et al. and Frenking et al.[4,23] In
conclusion, computations suggest that both p-3Cl12F+ and
p-3Br12F+ are stronger hydride ion abstractors than 15H+,
comparably strong as 15F+, but are still less electrophilic
compared to the fluorinated dialkyl chloronium salt [Cl-
(CH2CF3)2]+, whose HIA is over 100 kJ mol–1 higher
(Table 2).
To experimentally verify the unusually large HIAs and
demonstrate
the
new
synthons’
easy
handling,
both
p-3Cl12F+ and p-3Br12F+ were reacted with n-pentane and
n-butane
(Scheme 2).
Solutions
of
p-3Cl12F+
and
p-3Br12F+ were charged with an excess of the respective
alkane at low temperatures, brought to room temperature,
and monitored by NMR spectroscopy. After 30 minutes, a
slight discoloration of the reaction mixture was observed,
and after another 24 hours, a clear, light brown solution was
obtained.

obtained by slowly evaporating a concentrated solution in n-

Interestingly, solutions of the respective cationic species
p-3Cl12F+ or p-3Br12F+, that were kept at � 25°C and still
showed the expected signals in the 19F NMR spectrum, gave
the same reaction outcome as solutions that were kept at
ambient temperature and that were NMR silent. This
further proves the presence of the corresponding cationic
species in the NMR silent solutions at room temperature
and the high thermal stability of p-3Cl12F+ and p-3Br12F+
compared to their perfluorinated analog. Note that the
formed cationic alkyl species are not stable in the presence
of the chloro-gallate counter-anion. The respective alkyl
chloride species are assumed to be formed (Scheme 2). This
is based on the observation that in the case of the reaction
of 15F+[Ga2Cl7] with Et3SiH, where the methane 15F-H and
[Et3Si][Ga2Cl7] are formed, the latter immediately decom-
poses into Et3SiCl (see Supporting Information for more
Information). In conclusion, both p-3Cl12F+ and p-3Br12F+
proved to be powerful hydride abstraction agents that can
activate short-chain, linear alkanes like n-pentane and n-
butane. This reactivity was recently reported for the first
time using fluorinated dialkyl chloronium salts and was in
principle
known
from
Reed‘s
highly
electrophilic
CH3(CHB11Me5Br6).[9,21]
In this work, we introduced a more convenient access to
the perfluorinated trityl cation (15F+), which only involves
commercially available starting materials. Furthermore, we
introduced the halodefluorination in para-position of the
phenyl moieties using TMSX (X=Cl, Br), which enables the
generation of more stable, halogenated trityl derivatives
(p-3Cl12F+ and p-3Br12F+). Despite their high thermal
stability, both p-3Cl12F+ and p-3Br12F+ are still highly
potent hydride abstraction agents with similar strength as
the
15F+,
as
demonstrated
both
computationally
and
experimentally.
With
these
new,
easily
accessible
and
relatively stable species in hand, we provide a very useful
synthon for inorganic and organic synthetic chemistry, which
might allow the access into a new terra incognita of reactive
intermediates and cationic compounds.

Abstract: Herein, we present the easy-to-access syn- thesis of the perfluorotrityl cation (15F+) with commer- cial GaCl3 and the further functionalization of the para- fluorine atoms of 15F+ via halodefluorination using trimethylsilyl halides TMSX (X=Cl, Br). This gives access to equally reactive halogenated trityl derivatives (p-3Cl12F+ and p-3Br12F+), which can be handled at room temperature. The impact of the para-exchange on the electronic structure is determined by NMR and UV/ Vis spectroscopy. Finally, the new synthons’ high hydride ion affinities are demonstrated computationally and experimentally by hydride abstraction from the short-chain, linear alkanes n-pentane and n-butane. Hydride abstraction is a versatile yet challenging tool in synthesis due to its role in generating highly reactive species such as carbocations or other positively charged intermediates.[1] The latter are key compounds in many organic and inorganic reactions, which are not only of academic interest, but may also be industrially relevant.[2] A common reaction for such a hydride abstraction is often realized by the so-called trityl cation [C(C6H5)3]+ (in the following abbreviated as 15H+).[3] The three phenyl groups stabilize the positively charged central carbon atom and the relatively bulky ligands allow for its isolation.[2c] Due to the electron-deficient nature of the central carbon atom, the trityl cation is an effective reagent for hydride and alkyl abstractions and serves as a one-electron oxidant. However, as shown previously, its hydride ion affinity (HIA) can be further increased by fluorination of the phenyl moieties.[4] The perfluorinated counterpart [C(C6F5)3]+ (in the following abbreviated as 15F+) shows a considerably higher HIA ([C(C6F5)3]+ =955 kJmol� 1) than the non-fluorinated trityl cation ([C(C6H5)3]+ =801 kJmol� 1). Even though [C(C6F5)3]+ was first characterized by NMR spectroscopy in the 1960s by Filler and Olah as an intermediate in chemical reactions, its first isolation was not achieved until recently.[5–7] This was made possible by introducing the very robust and weakly coordinating anion (WCA) [Al- (OTeF5)4]� .[7] At the same time, a series of partially fluorinated trityl cations had been reported by Ozerov et al. as carborane-stabilized salts.[8a] Beforehand, a partially fluorinated trityl cation was already isolated by Reed et al., but not investigated further.[8b] The very high electrophilicity of the perfluorinated trityl cation was proven experimentally when it enabled the generation of the tert-butyl cation through hydride ion abstraction from isobutane and showed its high oxidation potential by the synthesis of a magic blue derivative.[7] Very recently, it was shown that fluorinated chloronium ions could even exceed the hydride ion affinity by more than 100 kJmol–1 and can activate short-chain, linear alkanes, e.g., n-pentane.[9] However, the synthetic access and application of these fluorinated trityl cations and chloronium ions have been limited so far by their synthetic accessibility due to the non- commonly available WCAs. As M. Ingleson recently pointed out, “a simpler route to access these fluorinated trityl salts would be really useful for the community”.[10] Hence, our group has developed an easier and more straightforward way to prepare this compound. Herein, we present the easy-to-access synthesis of the perfluorotrityl cation (15F+) and the further functionalization of its para- fluorine atoms via halodefluorination using trimethylsilyl halides TMSX (X=Cl, Br). This enables the synthesis of more stable yet equally reactive halogenated trityl deriva- tives (p-3Cl12F+ and p-3Br12F+). Right before the publica- tion of this work, an article by Ozerov et al. has been published that reports on the stabilization of the perfluoro- trityl cation at room temperature using halogenated carbor- ane WCAs.[8c] The addition of 0.5 equivalents of PhF 3CCl to a colorless solution of GaCl3 in SO2ClF at � 80°C results in an immediate color change to berry-red and the appearance of three signals in the low-temperature 19F NMR spectrum at � 108.7, � 123.7, and � 150.9 ppm (Scheme 1, Figure S1). These signals can be assigned to the para-, ortho-, and meta- fluorine atoms of 15F+.
